class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 gUPbkQ sc-5xdgy4-1 lZhyG">By<!-- --> <a style="text-decoration:none" data-testid="author-name-link" href="/author/rachel-stultsDISABLED/">Rachel Stults</a></p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 jjdjXe date-text"><time dateTime="2022-08-01T11:00:15.000Z">August 1, 2022</time></p></div></div></header><div><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">It's a slow Sunday morning. You've just brewed your Nespresso and popped open your laptop to check out the latest home listings before you hit the road for a day of open houses.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">You're DIYing this real estate thing, and you think you're doing pretty well—after all, any info you might need is at your fingertips online, right? That and your own sterling judgment.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Oh, dear home buyer (or seller!)—we know you <em>can</em> do it on your own. But you really, really shouldn't. This is likely the biggest financial decision of your entire life, and you need a Realtor® if you want to do it right. Here's why.</p><div data-testid="iframe-widget" class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 cGIhfE"><iframe height="230px" style="width:100%;border:0" src="https://www.realtor.com/creative/rdc-ads/local-listings-widget/" loading="lazy" title="Embedded widget"></iframe></div><div class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 cGIhfE"><p>[jwplatform rqZPgCIU]</p>
</div><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">1. They have the right expertise</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Want to check the <em>MLS</em> for a <em>4B/2B</em> with an <em>EIK</em> and a <em>W/D</em>? <a target="_blank" href="https://www.realtor.com/tag/learning-the-lingo/">Real estate has its own language</a>, full of acronyms and semi-arcane jargon, and your Realtor is trained to speak that language fluently.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Plus, buying or selling a home usually requires dozens of forms, reports, disclosures, and other technical documents. Realtors have the expertise to help you prepare a killer deal—while avoiding delays or costly mistakes that can seriously mess you up.</p><div data-testid="iframe-widget" class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 cGIhfE"><iframe height="230px" style="width:100%;border:0" src="https://www.realtor.com/creative/rdc-ads/search-listings-widget/" loading="lazy" title="Embedded widget"></iframe></div><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">2. They have turbocharged searching power</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">The Internet is awesome. You can find almost anything—<em>anything!</em> And with online real estate listing sites such as yours truly, you can find up-to-date home listings on your own, any time you want. But guess what? Realtors have access to <em>even more</em> listings. Sometimes properties are available but not actively advertised. A Realtor can help you find those hidden gems.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Plus, a good local Realtor is going to know the search area way better than you ever could. Have your eye on a particular neighborhood, but it's just out of your price range? Your Realtor is equipped to know the ins and outs of <em>every</em> neighborhood, so she can direct you toward a home in your price range that you may have overlooked.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">3. They have bullish negotiating chops</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Any time you buy or sell a home, you're going to encounter negotiations—and as today's housing market heats up, those negotiations are more likely than ever to get a little heated.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">You can expect lots of competition, cutthroat tactics, all-cash offers, and <a target="_blank" href="https://www.realtor.com/advice/buy/on-the-house-how-to-make-your-offer-more-competitive/">bidding wars</a>. Don't you want a savvy and professional negotiator on your side to seal the best deal for you?</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">And it's not just about how much money you end up spending or netting. A Realtor will help draw up a purchase agreement that allows enough time for inspections, contingencies, and anything else that's crucial to your particular needs.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">4. They're connected to <em>everyone</em></h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Realtors might not know everything, but they make it their mission to know just about everyone who can possibly help in the process of buying or selling a home. Mortgage brokers, real estate attorneys, home inspectors, home stagers, interior designers—the list goes on—and they're all in your Realtor's network. Use them.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">5. They adhere to a strict code of ethics</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Not every real estate agent is a Realtor, who is a licensed real estate salesperson who belongs to the National Association of Realtors®, the largest trade group in the country.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">What difference does it make? Realtors are held to a higher ethical standard than licensed agents and must adhere to a <a rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank" href="http://www.realtor.org/governance/governing-documents/the-code-of-ethics">Code of Ethics</a>.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">6. They're your sage parent/data analyst/therapist—all rolled into one</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">The thing about Realtors: They wear a lot of different hats. Sure, they're salespeople, but they actually do a whole heck of a lot to <a target="_blank" href="https://www.realtor.com/advice/buy/what-realtors-do-to-earn-commission/">earn their commission</a>. They're constantly driving around, checking out listings for you. They spend their own money on marketing your home (if you're selling). They're researching comps to make sure you're getting the best deal.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">And, of course, they're working for you at nearly all hours of the day and night—whether you need more info on a home or just someone to talk to in order to feel at ease with the offer you just put in. This is the biggest financial (and possibly emotional) decision of your life, and guiding you through it isn't a responsibility Realtors take lightly.</p><div data-testid="mrc-mortgage-widget"><div data-mrc="main-content-MrcMortgageEmbed-27" class="mrc-inline"></div></div></div><div class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 dGraMb"><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 hxcYYy">Rachel Stults is the managing editor at Realtor.com and co-host of the Realtor.com podcast "House Party." You've just brewed your Nespresso and popped open your laptop to check out the latest home listings before you hit the road for a day of open houses. You're DIYing this real estate thing, and you think you're doing pretty well—after all, any info you might need is at your fingertips online, right? That and your own sterling judgment. Oh, dear home buyer (or seller!)—we know you  can do it on your own. But you really, really shouldn't. This is likely the biggest financial decision of your entire life, and you need a Realtor® if you want to do it right. Here's why. [jwplatform rqZPgCIU] 1. They have the right expertise Want to check the MLS for a 4B/2B with an EIK and a W/D ? Real estate has its own language , full of acronyms and semi-arcane jargon, and your Realtor is trained to speak that language fluently. Plus, buying or selling a home usually requires dozens of forms, reports, disclosures, and other technical documents. Realtors have the expertise to help you prepare a killer deal—while avoiding delays or costly mistakes that can seriously mess you up. 2. They have turbocharged searching power The Internet is awesome. You can find almost anything— anything! And with online real estate listing sites such as yours truly, you can find up-to-date home listings on your own, any time you want. But guess what? Realtors have access to even more listings. Sometimes properties are available but not actively advertised. A Realtor can help you find those hidden gems. Plus, a good local Realtor is going to know the search area way better than you ever could. Have your eye on a particular neighborhood, but it's just out of your price range? Your Realtor is equipped to know the ins and outs of  every neighborhood, so she can direct you toward a home in your price range that you may have overlooked. 3. They have bullish negotiating chops Any time you buy or sell a home, you're going to encounter negotiations—and as today's housing market heats up, those negotiations are more likely than ever to get a little heated. You can expect lots of competition, cutthroat tactics, all-cash offers, and bidding wars . Don't you want a savvy and professional negotiator on your side to seal the best deal for you? And it's not just about how much money you end up spending or netting. A Realtor will help draw up a purchase agreement that allows enough time for inspections, contingencies, and anything else that's crucial to your particular needs. 4. They're connected to everyone Realtors might not know everything, but they make it their mission to know just about everyone who can possibly help in the process of buying or selling a home. Mortgage brokers, real estate attorneys, home inspectors, home stagers, interior designers—the list goes on—and they're all in your Realtor's network. Use them. 5. They adhere to a strict code of ethics Not every real estate agent is a Realtor, who is a licensed real estate salesperson who belongs to the National Association of Realtors®, the largest trade group in the country. What difference does it make? Realtors are held to a higher ethical standard than licensed agents and must adhere to a Code of Ethics . 6. They're your sage parent/data analyst/therapist—all rolled into one The thing about Realtors: They wear a lot of different hats. Sure, they're salespeople, but they actually do a whole heck of a lot to earn their commission . They're constantly driving around, checking out listings for you. They spend their own money on marketing your home (if you're selling). They're researching comps to make sure you're getting the best deal. And, of course, they're working for you at nearly all hours of the day and night—whether you need more info on a home or just someone to talk to in order to feel at ease with the offer you just put in. This is the biggest financial (and possibly emotional) decision of your life, and guiding you through it isn't a responsibility Realtors take lightly. Here are the coverages included in most standard homeowners policies. Cost to rebuild your home This is the cost to rebuild your home at today's current price. It is not the selling price or market value. Other structures on your property Coverage for structures not attached to your home (shed, detached garage, etc.) Personal property Provides coverage for personal items, such as furniture, clothes, sporting goods, and electronics. Living expenses Covers additional living expenses you may incur if you are unable to live in your house due to a loss. Personal liability Helps protect you and helps cover legal costs if a claim is made or a suit is brought against you. Medical payments Covers medical expenses for individuals not in your household, for injuries that occurred while on your property. About Renting You Should Stop Believing Immediately</h1></div></div><div class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 iLRUXc"><div class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 cwbAsu author-section"><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 gUPbkQ sc-5xdgy4-1 lZhyG">By<!-- --> <a style="text-decoration:none" data-testid="author-name-link" href="/author/jenny-buttaccio/">Jenny Lelwica Buttaccio</a></p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 jjdjXe date-text"><time dateTime="2022-08-11T10:30:03.000Z">August 11, 2022</time></p></div></div></header><div><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Years ago, I discovered cockroaches in my Chicago apartment. I spent money on sprays, traps, and other <a target="_blank" href="https://www.realtor.com/advice/home-improvement/pest-control-mistakes-youre-making/">pest control</a> gadgets to rid my place of the disgusting rent-free tenants, but I was no match for them.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">So I turned to my landlord for help. If he refused, I’d withhold rent or break my lease—I was justified, right?</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Maybe. Maybe not. Rental laws and tenant rights vary from city to city, and it actually might not have been OK for me to up and leave—even if my landlord wasn't getting the job done. (Thankfully, it didn't come to that: He quickly hired an exterminator, and I lived out the remainder of my lease roach-free.)</p><div data-testid="iframe-widget" class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 cGIhfE"><iframe height="230px" style="width:100%;border:0" src="https://www.realtor.com/creative/rdc-ads/local-listings-widget/" loading="lazy" title="Embedded widget"></iframe></div><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">But like I did, many tenants believe that you can simply deduct or skip rent for problems or repairs—which is just not true. And there are other myths about renting that are widely believed. Here are some of the most common ones—and the truth behind them.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">1. You’ll never land an apartment with a bad credit score</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Yes, bad credit <em>can</em> make things more challenging, especially in a competitive rental market. But it doesn’t automatically disqualify you as a rental candidate.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">When you fill out an application for housing, you’ll undergo a credit and background check. But other factors—such as applying with a roommate, proof of pay stubs, or letters of recommendation from your previous landlords—may <a target="_blank" href="https://www.realtor.com/advice/rent/how-to-rent-with-bad-credit/">help seal the deal</a>.</p><div data-testid="iframe-widget" class="Boxstyles__StyledBox-rui__sc-1p1qqov-0 cGIhfE"><iframe height="230px" style="width:100%;border:0" src="https://www.realtor.com/creative/rdc-ads/search-listings-widget/" loading="lazy" title="Embedded widget"></iframe></div><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">2. The longer you've lived somewhere, the greater the chances you'll lose your security deposit</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">So you've lived in a place for only a year, and there's no damage to speak of—you'll probably get your security deposit back, right? But if you've lived there longer, you're probably thinking you can kiss that deposit goodbye.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">It isn't always so cut and dried, says <strong>Megan Perkins Roldan</strong>, property manager at Chestnut Tower Apartments in Chicago.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">“We definitely take into account the length of tenancy when assessing wear-and-tear damages and expect that longer-term residents will need more work from us at move-out," Roldan says. "But it’s not necessarily [considered] damage.”</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">The best way to avoid charges is to leave the unit in the condition it was when you moved in, whenever that was. Do a deep clean, patch large holes, and repaint any custom-colored walls.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">3. Your landlord can evict you for any reason</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">If you're on a signed lease, a landlord typically can’t evict you for any reason. The landlord must show sufficient evidence that you’ve broken the lease agreement, and your eviction is justifiable. (If you're renting month to month, however, the rules get a little fuzzy.)</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">What's more: You shouldn't come home to find the locks changed and your stuff out on the street. To evict a resident, landlords or property management companies must provide sufficient and specific written notice, according to <a rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank" href="https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/evictions-renters-tenants-rights-29824.html">Nolo</a>, one of the largest online libraries of legal information for consumers.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">If you fail to move or change your behavior after receiving the notice, the landlord has the legal right to proceed with a lawsuit to evict you.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">4. A landlord is responsible for all repairs and maintenance</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">The responsibilities of the landlord or property manager vary depending on where you live and the terms of your lease. In general, your landlord is on the hook to handle such things as general maintenance, noise complaints, plumbing issues, and pest control.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">But there are some things that simply aren't your landlord's problem—usually if it's something caused by <em>you.</em></p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">“If the damage is due to the tenant's negligence, the landlord might choose to address the repairs and withhold the cost of the repairs out of the tenant's security deposit," says <strong>Daniel L. Staley</strong>, associate broker at Staley Real Estate in Rhinebeck, NY.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">And, if damages are severe enough, it could cost you more than your security deposit—we're talking lawsuits.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">5. You can deduct rent when you do your own repairs or maintenance</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">While it might seem easiest to just subtract the money you spent on repairs, this could get you into trouble down the road—especially if you haven’t discussed this arrangement with your landlord.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Leave the work to your landlord, and make sure to send him an itemized list of what needs to be done. That way, if the landlord refuses to do the repairs, you have ammo to take to a higher power.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Renters can call their local building inspectors "to inspect [the place] and force the landlord to make the repairs that are required by code,” says <strong>Alicia Bosben</strong>, broker property manager at the Realty Tree in Madison, WI.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">6. Rental prices are set in stone</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">We won't lie: You don't typically have much bargaining power when it comes to how much you'll pay—especially in a hot rental market. But each landlord is different, and you do have a few tricks up your sleeve.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">First, consider a longer lease. Landlords don't usually want to deal with turnover. If you can commit to being in for the long(er) haul, they might be more willing to negotiate the rental price and lease terms.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Second, consider your time frame. There are typically more rental vacancies in winter, so landlords might be more inclined to strike a deal at that time.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Finally, arm yourself with info to help your case: Know the vacancy rate and the going rate for similar units in the area, and bring recommendation letters from your current landlord to show you're a good tenant.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">7. Landlords can enter your place whenever they want</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">A landlord may need to enter your unit for a variety of reasons—to show your unit to prospective tenants, to check the fire alarms, or simply to do routine maintenance.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">But legally, a landlord can’t enter your apartment whenever he wants. He must provide you with sufficient warning, generally 24 hours.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">There are some exceptions, of course: If there's an emergency—like fire or a sever water leak—landlords can enter without notice.</p><h2 class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 eAPYSB">8. You’re flushing away money by renting</h2><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">Sure, buying a home is a good investment. But there are a ton of reasons why renting isn't a <em>bad</em> investment.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">It might be better for you financially, you might like having someone on call for maintenance and repairs, or perhaps you simply want the flexibility to up and move whenever you want. Plus, renting can allow you time to save for a down payment on that house.</p><p class="base__StyledType-rui__sc-18muj27-0 IEPPf sc-7dicpk-0 ccZqsH core-paragraph">So the next time well-intentioned friends or family members try to tell you that renting is a bad move, tell them it's a myth—and you can debunk it.</p><a target="_blank" data-testid="text-widget" class="sc-s4khec-0 jknOCu" I spent money on sprays, traps, and other pest control  gadgets to rid my place of the disgusting rent-free tenants, but I was no match for them. So I turned to my landlord for help. If he refused, I’d withhold rent or break my lease—I was justified, right? Maybe. Maybe not. Rental laws and tenant rights vary from city to city, and it actually might not have been OK for me to up and leave—even if my landlord wasn't getting the job done. (Thankfully, it didn't come to that: He quickly hired an exterminator, and I lived out the remainder of my lease roach-free.) But like I did, many tenants believe that you can simply deduct or skip rent for problems or repairs—which is just not true. And there are other myths about renting that are widely believed. Here are some of the most common ones—and the truth behind them. 1. You’ll never land an apartment with a bad credit score Yes, bad credit can make things more challenging, especially in a competitive rental market. But it doesn’t automatically disqualify you as a rental candidate. When you fill out an application for housing, you’ll undergo a credit and background check. But other factors—such as applying with a roommate, proof of pay stubs, or letters of recommendation from your previous landlords—may help seal the deal . 2. The longer you've lived somewhere, the greater the chances you'll lose your security deposit So you've lived in a place for only a year, and there's no damage to speak of—you'll probably get your security deposit back, right? But if you've lived there longer, you're probably thinking you can kiss that deposit goodbye. It isn't always so cut and dried, says  Megan Perkins Roldan , property manager at Chestnut Tower Apartments in Chicago. “We definitely take into account the length of tenancy when assessing wear-and-tear damages and expect that longer-term residents will need more work from us at move-out," Roldan says. "But it’s not necessarily [considered] damage.” The best way to avoid charges is to leave the unit in the condition it was when you moved in, whenever that was. Do a deep clean, patch large holes, and repaint any custom-colored walls. 3. Your landlord can evict you for any reason If you're on a signed lease, a landlord typically can’t evict you for any reason. The landlord must show sufficient evidence that you’ve broken the lease agreement, and your eviction is justifiable. (If you're renting month to month, however, the rules get a little fuzzy.) What's more: You shouldn't come home to find the locks changed and your stuff out on the street. To evict a resident, landlords or property management companies must provide sufficient and specific written notice, according to Nolo , one of the largest online libraries of legal information for consumers. If you fail to move or change your behavior after receiving the notice, the landlord has the legal right to proceed with a lawsuit to evict you. 4. A landlord is responsible for all repairs and maintenance The responsibilities of the landlord or property manager vary depending on where you live and the terms of your lease. In general, your landlord is on the hook to handle such things as general maintenance, noise complaints, plumbing issues, and pest control. But there are some things that simply aren't your landlord's problem—usually if it's something caused by you. “If the damage is due to the tenant's negligence, the landlord might choose to address the repairs and withhold the cost of the repairs out of the tenant's security deposit," says  Daniel L. Staley , associate broker at Staley Real Estate in Rhinebeck, NY. And, if damages are severe enough, it could cost you more than your security deposit—we're talking lawsuits. 5. You can deduct rent when you do your own repairs or maintenance While it might seem easiest to just subtract the money you spent on repairs, this could get you into trouble down the road—especially if you haven’t discussed this arrangement with your landlord. Leave the work to your landlord, and make sure to send him an itemized list of what needs to be done. That way, if the landlord refuses to do the repairs, you have ammo to take to a higher power. Renters can call their local building inspectors "to inspect [the place] and force the landlord to make the repairs that are required by code,” says  Alicia Bosben , broker property manager at the Realty Tree in Madison, WI. 6. Rental prices are set in stone We won't lie: You don't typically have much bargaining power when it comes to how much you'll pay—especially in a hot rental market. But each landlord is different, and you do have a few tricks up your sleeve. First, consider a longer lease. Landlords don't usually want to deal with turnover. If you can commit to being in for the long(er) haul, they might be more willing to negotiate the rental price and lease terms. Second, consider your time frame. There are typically more rental vacancies in winter, so landlords might be more inclined to strike a deal at that time. Finally, arm yourself with info to help your case: Know the vacancy rate and the going rate for similar units in the area, and bring recommendation letters from your current landlord to show you're a good tenant. 7. Landlords can enter your place whenever they want A landlord may need to enter your unit for a variety of reasons—to show your unit to prospective tenants, to check the fire alarms, or simply to do routine maintenance. But legally, a landlord can’t enter your apartment whenever he wants. He must provide you with sufficient warning, generally 24 hours. There are some exceptions, of course: If there's an emergency—like fire or a sever water leak—landlords can enter without notice. 8. You’re flushing away money by renting Sure, buying a home is a good investment. But there are a ton of reasons why renting isn't a bad investment. It might be better for you financially, you might like having someone on call for maintenance and repairs, or perhaps you simply want the flexibility to up and move whenever you want. Plus, renting can allow you time to save for a down payment on that house. So the next time well-intentioned friends or family members try to tell you that renting is a bad move, tell them it's a myth—and you can debunk it. Manage your rentals like a pro. 	<div class="entry-content">

		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Realtor.com delivered sustainable growth throughout FY26, outpacing the market and our competitors</span><span style="font-weight: 400;">. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">In Q4, we saw a 13% increase in revenue – our seventh consecutive quarter of growth, and third consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. <article id="post-3119" class="post-3119 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-realtor-com-news tag-company-updates tag-damian-eales tag-news-corp-earnings tag-realtor-com-ceo tag-realtor-com-earnings">
		<header class="entry-header">
		<h2 class="entry-title"><a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/realtor-com-posts-sixth-quarter-of-revenue-growth/" rel="bookmark">FY26 Q3 (Jan – March) Earnings: Realtor.com Posts Sixth Straight Quarter of Revenue Growth</a></h2>	</header><!-- .entry-header -->

	    
			<div class="post-thumbnail">
			<a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/realtor-com-posts-sixth-quarter-of-revenue-growth/"  style="background-image:url( https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/GettyImages-1138742797.jpeg );">
                			</a>
		</div><!-- .post-thumbnail -->
	
	<div class="entry-content">
        <span class="author-badge">
        	<img src="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581-130x150.jpg" width="111" height="128" srcset="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581.jpg 2x" alt="Damian Eales" class="avatar avatar-128 wp-user-avatar wp-user-avatar-128 alignnone photo" />                            <div class="entry-meta">
                    <strong>by <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/author/deales/">Damian Eales</a></strong>
                    on 7th May 2026                </div><!-- .entry-meta -->
                        </span>
		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">In FY26 Q3, Realtor.com delivered 10% revenue growth, its sixth consecutive quarter of growth. We remained the second most visited U.S. real estate portal, according to Comscore. We averaged 261 million monthly site visits, a 31% share of the market, </span><span style="font-weight: 400;">compared to only 12% for Redfin and 6% for Homes.com. </span><span style="font-weight: 400;">We also increased our lead in engagement – Realtor.com averaged 5.3 visits per unique user, compared to 4.8 in Q2, outperforming Zillow by 1.5x (3.5 visits/UU), Redfin by 1.8x (2.9 visits/UU), and Homes.com by 2.8x (at 1.9 visits/UU).</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">We continued to execute against our product roadmap. In March, we launched the </span><a href="https://mediaroom.realtor.com/2026-03-30-Search-Homes-and-See-What-You-Can-Afford-with-the-New-Realtor-com-R-App-in-ChatGPT" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Realtor.com app in ChatGPT</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> to simplify the pre-search stage of homebuying and reach a new incremental audience for our clients. We also unveiled the </span><a href="https://www.realtor.com/research/what-is-the-market-clock/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Realtor.com Market Clock</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;">, which gives professionals and consumers a clear, visual read on whether a local market favors buyers or sellers. On the industry side, we are seeing strong early momentum behind </span><a href="https://www.realtor.com/plus-learn/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span style="font-weight: 400;">Realtor.com+</span></a><span style="font-weight: 400;"> with continued MLS signings and strong agent adoption.</span></p>
<p> <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/realtor-com-posts-sixth-quarter-of-revenue-growth/#more-3119" class="more-link">… Continue reading<span class="screen-reader-text"> “FY26 Q3 (Jan – March) Earnings: Realtor.com Posts Sixth Straight Quarter of Revenue Growth”</span></a></p>
	</div><!-- .entry-content -->

	
</article><!-- #post-## -->


<article id="post-3116" class="post-3116 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-realtor-com-news tag-damian-eales tag-listing-fragmentation tag-open-marketplace tag-private-marketplaces tag-realtor-com-preview tag-realtor-com-preview-listings tag-zillow-preview-listings">
		<header class="entry-header">
		<h2 class="entry-title"><a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/more-exposure-less-fragmentation/" rel="bookmark">More Exposure, Less Fragmentation: Why Realtor.com Is Opening Preview Listings to More Buyers</a></h2>	</header><!-- .entry-header -->

	    
			<div class="post-thumbnail">
			<a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/more-exposure-less-fragmentation/"  style="background-image:url( https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/GettyImages-528689860-scaled.jpeg );">
                			</a>
		</div><!-- .post-thumbnail -->
	
	<div class="entry-content">
        <span class="author-badge">
        	<img src="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581-130x150.jpg" width="111" height="128" srcset="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581.jpg 2x" alt="Damian Eales" class="avatar avatar-128 wp-user-avatar wp-user-avatar-128 alignnone photo" />                            <div class="entry-meta">
                    <strong>by <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/author/deales/">Damian Eales</a></strong>
                    on 5th May 2026                </div><!-- .entry-meta -->
                        </span>
		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">For 30 years, Realtor.com has enabled an open marketplace where listings are transparent and broadly accessible to consumers. That model is something the rest of the world envies. It gives sellers extraordinary exposure at no cost, gives buyers broad access to homes for sale and the data they need to inform their purchase, and has kept real estate professionals at the center of the transaction.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Markets are always evolving, but our principles stay the same: we support listing transparency; we advocate for independent buyer representation; and we enable real estate agents to fulfill their fiduciary duty to their buyers or sellers. It’s through this lens that we make all of our decisions, including to display Realtor.com Preview Listings sourced from Zillow. </span> <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/more-exposure-less-fragmentation/#more-3116" class="more-link">… Continue reading<span class="screen-reader-text"> “More Exposure, Less Fragmentation: Why Realtor.com Is Opening Preview Listings to More Buyers”</span></a></p>
	</div><!-- .entry-content -->

	
</article><!-- #post-## -->

		<header class="entry-header">

			<div class="post-thumbnail">
			<a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/realtor-com-app-in-chatgpt/"  style="background-image:url( https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/GettyImages-1317965457.jpeg );">
                			</a>
		</div><!-- .post-thumbnail -->
	
	<div class="entry-content">
        <span class="author-badge">
        	<img src="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Mickey2021-150x150.jpg" width="128" height="128" srcset="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Mickey2021-scaled.jpg 2x" alt="Mickey Neuberger" class="avatar avatar-128 wp-user-avatar wp-user-avatar-128 alignnone photo" />                            <div class="entry-meta">

                    on 30th March 2026                </div><!-- .entry-meta -->
                        </span>
		<p>Today, I’m proud to share the launch of the Realtor.com app in ChatGPT. This new conversational experience helps guide consumers through the “pre-search” phase, that critical, often-overwhelming window where buyers tackle big-picture questions about affordability and lifestyle. There, you can immerse yourself in visuals, including videos, photos, floorplans, and our FlyAround feature, and leverage deep market insights that help you truly understand the homes you’re looking at before you connect with an agent.</p>

<article id="post-3099" class="post-3099 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-realtor-com-news tag-coming-soon tag-mls tag-mls-partnership">
		<header class="entry-header">
		<h2 class="entry-title"><a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/sellers-deserve-clicks-not-cliques/" rel="bookmark">Sellers Deserve Clicks, Not Cliques: Why Maximum Exposure Wins</a></h2>	</header><!-- .entry-header -->

	    
			<div class="post-thumbnail">
			<a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/sellers-deserve-clicks-not-cliques/"  style="background-image:url( https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/GettyImages-588954624.jpeg );">
                			</a>
		</div><!-- .post-thumbnail -->
	
	<div class="entry-content">
        <span class="author-badge">
        	<img src="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Icon-Realtor-Color.png" width="96" height="96" srcset="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Icon-Realtor-Color.png 2x" alt="Realtor.com" class="avatar avatar-128 wp-user-avatar wp-user-avatar-128 alignnone photo" />                            <div class="entry-meta">
                    <strong>by <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/author/realtorcontribu/">Realtor.com</a></strong>
                    on 18th March 2026                </div><!-- .entry-meta -->
                        </span>
		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Sellers want </span><i><span style="font-weight: 400;">clicks</span></i><span style="font-weight: 400;">, not </span><i><span style="font-weight: 400;">cliques</span></i><span style="font-weight: 400;">. We believe sellers are best served by maximizing exposure to their listing either as a ‘Coming Soon’ listing, or a ‘For Sale’ listing in their MLS. Sellers should be wary of advice that they should limit their advertising campaign to any one portal or brokerage, resulting in fewer buyers, when they can freely promote their property on all portals, at no cost. </span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">We understand a seller’s desire for price exploration and we believe a ‘Coming Soon’ listing is the best way to do that. Using the ‘Coming Soon’ status and advertising these properties to the full open market solves the challenge of achieving price discovery without starting the days-on-market clock and eliminates the need for private marketplaces. ‘Coming Soon’ ensures a fair marketplace where every buyer has equal access to all listings and all information about the property, and every seller has maximum exposure for their home, leading to more eyeballs, more bidders, more offers and oftentimes a higher sale price. </span> <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/sellers-deserve-clicks-not-cliques/#more-3099" class="more-link">… Continue reading<span class="screen-reader-text"> “Sellers Deserve Clicks, Not Cliques: Why Maximum Exposure Wins”</span></a></p>
	</div><!-- .entry-content -->

	
</article><!-- #post-## -->

		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Just one month ago we introduced Realtor.com+ with a clear mission: to build a collaborative search platform that keeps the industry, and the agent, at the center of the experience. The response has been nothing short of incredible.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">I’m thrilled to share that we are already expanding Realtor.com+, signing two major California MLSs and bringing the total number of participating MLSs to 18. <article id="post-3090" class="post-3090 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-leadership-perspectives tag-damian-eales tag-realtor-com-ceo tag-realtor-com-earnings">
		<header class="entry-header">
		<h2 class="entry-title"><a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/the-most-engaged-audience-in-the-industry/" rel="bookmark">FY26 Q2 (Oct – Dec) Earnings: The Most Engaged Audience in the Industry Driving Continued Revenue Growth</a></h2>	</header><!-- .entry-header -->

	    
			<div class="post-thumbnail">
			<a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/the-most-engaged-audience-in-the-industry/"  style="background-image:url( https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/GettyImages-1452725741.jpeg );">
                			</a>
		</div><!-- .post-thumbnail -->
	
	<div class="entry-content">
        <span class="author-badge">
        	<img src="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581-130x150.jpg" width="111" height="128" srcset="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581.jpg 2x" alt="Damian Eales" class="avatar avatar-128 wp-user-avatar wp-user-avatar-128 alignnone photo" />                            <div class="entry-meta">
                    <strong>by <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/author/deales/">Damian Eales</a></strong>
                    on 5th February 2026                </div><!-- .entry-meta -->
                        </span>
		<h4><b>Strong quarterly audience and revenue</b></h4>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">In our fiscal second quarter¹, Realtor.com delivered exceptional results. According to the independent industry measure, Comscore²</span><span style="font-weight: 400;">, we drove 3.4X the visit share of Homes.com and 2.3X Redfin, while rapidly catching Zillow by closing more than half the visit share gap over the past 18-months. We remained No. 1 in audience engagement — the measure we consider most associated with buyer intent. At 4.8 visits per unique visitor we are materially ahead of our closest competitors.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Our powerful audience is increasingly a result of being part of News Corp. We expertly leverage trusted brands—including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, MarketWatch, The Sun U.S., The New York Post, and most recently, the California Post—to strategically extend our brand and content reach to generate high-intent buyers for the listings on our site.</span> <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/the-most-engaged-audience-in-the-industry/#more-3090" class="more-link">… Continue reading<span class="screen-reader-text"> “FY26 Q2 (Oct – Dec) Earnings: The Most Engaged Audience in the Industry Driving Continued Revenue Growth”</span></a></p>
	</div><!-- .entry-content -->

	
</article><!-- #post-## -->


<article id="post-3080" class="post-3080 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-leadership-perspectives tag-damian-eales tag-housing-supply tag-lack-of-affordability tag-let-america-built tag-realtor-com-ceo">
		<header class="entry-header">
		<h2 class="entry-title"><a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/from-conflict-to-concrete/" rel="bookmark">From Conflict to Concrete: A New Year’s Resolution</a></h2>	</header><!-- .entry-header -->

	    
			<div class="post-thumbnail">
			<a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/from-conflict-to-concrete/"  style="background-image:url( https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/GettyImages-638569788.jpeg );">
                			</a>
		</div><!-- .post-thumbnail -->
	
	<div class="entry-content">
        <span class="author-badge">
        	<img src="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581-130x150.jpg" width="111" height="128" srcset="https://corpblog.wpengine.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/DamianEales1-scaled-e1724855765581.jpg 2x" alt="Damian Eales" class="avatar avatar-128 wp-user-avatar wp-user-avatar-128 alignnone photo" />                            <div class="entry-meta">
                    <strong>by <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/author/deales/">Damian Eales</a></strong>
                    on 29th December 2025                </div><!-- .entry-meta -->
                        </span>
		<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Colleagues,</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">As we approach a new year, I am asking our industry to make one resolution: let’s recommit ourselves to a shared purpose that unites us – fighting for access for the American homeowner.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">Ours is an industry built on problem solving. Yet, too often lately it has been beset by bickering. We have exhausted our energy debating the merits of Clear Cooperation and the demerits of private listings. These debates, while legitimate, have  become distractions from larger challenges, and while we argue over how to slice a shrinking pie, millions of Americans are starving for a slice of the American Dream.</span></p>
<p><span style="font-weight: 400;">It is time to trade our discord for a common chorus. We must align on the one issue that truly matters: Housing Supply. </span> <a href="https://www.realtor.com/homemade/from-conflict-to-concrete/#more-3080" class="more-link">… Continue reading<span class="screen-reader-text"> “From Conflict to Concrete: A New Year’s Resolution”</span></a></p>
	</div><!-- .entry-content -->

	
</article><!-- #post-## -->

In Q4, we saw a 13% increase in revenue – our seventh consecutive quarter of growth, and third consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. We also outpaced competitors with the highest year-over-year gains in site visits and visits per unique user. Realtor.com averaged almost 300 million monthly visits last quarter – reaching a 33% market share – nearly 7x the visit share of Homes.com and 2.5x of Redfin, according to ComScore¹ We once again led our competitive set in engagement, generating 5.5 visits per unique user, significantly ahead of Zillow (3.6), Redfin (3.4) and Homes.com (1.9). Rising visit share, industry-leading engagement, and growing revenue all add up to consumers finding what they need, and more opportunity flowing to the agents who serve them. It’s exactly what we set out to build three years ago. … Continue reading “Realtor.com Concludes FY26 with Seventh Consecutive Quarter of Revenue Growth” How we’re rebuilding home search around how people actually buy homes by Dave Herman on 22nd July 2026 Buying a home is one of the most important decisions people make. And yet the tools we’ve historically given home buyers have often felt fragmented and transactional. Over the past several months, our team has been focused on a simple question: What would home search look like if it actually matched how people make decisions? Not just how they filter listings, but how they explore, ask questions, collaborate, and build confidence along the way. … Continue reading “How we’re rebuilding home search around how people actually buy homes” Introducing RealAssist™ AI: From First Question to Closing by Mickey Neuberger on 2nd June 2026 Today is a big day for us at Realtor.com. We’re launching RealAssist™ AI and I genuinely believe it’s one of the smartest, most powerful tools we’ve ever put in a buyer’s hands, one that will only get better over time. Developed in collaboration with Google and grounded in nearly 30 years of Realtor.com buyer intelligence, it guides home buyers from their very first question all the way to closing. Not just search. The whole journey. … Continue reading “Introducing RealAssist™ AI: From First Question to Closing” FY26 Q3 (Jan – March) Earnings: Realtor.com Posts Sixth Straight Quarter of Revenue Growth by Damian Eales on 7th May 2026 In FY26 Q3, Realtor.com delivered 10% revenue growth, its sixth consecutive quarter of growth. We remained the second most visited U.S. real estate portal, according to Comscore. We averaged 261 million monthly site visits, a 31% share of the market, compared to only 12% for Redfin and 6% for Homes.com. We also increased our lead in engagement – Realtor.com averaged 5.3 visits per unique user, compared to 4.8 in Q2, outperforming Zillow by 1.5x (3.5 visits/UU), Redfin by 1.8x (2.9 visits/UU), and Homes.com by 2.8x (at 1.9 visits/UU). We continued to execute against our product roadmap. In March, we launched the Realtor.com app in ChatGPT to simplify the pre-search stage of homebuying and reach a new incremental audience for our clients. We also unveiled the Realtor.com Market Clock , which gives professionals and consumers a clear, visual read on whether a local market favors buyers or sellers. On the industry side, we are seeing strong early momentum behind Realtor.com+ with continued MLS signings and strong agent adoption. … Continue reading “FY26 Q3 (Jan – March) Earnings: Realtor.com Posts Sixth Straight Quarter of Revenue Growth” More Exposure, Less Fragmentation: Why Realtor.com Is Opening Preview Listings to More Buyers by Damian Eales on 5th May 2026 For 30 years, Realtor.com has enabled an open marketplace where listings are transparent and broadly accessible to consumers. That model is something the rest of the world envies. It gives sellers extraordinary exposure at no cost, gives buyers broad access to homes for sale and the data they need to inform their purchase, and has kept real estate professionals at the center of the transaction. Markets are always evolving, but our principles stay the same: we support listing transparency; we advocate for independent buyer representation; and we enable real estate agents to fulfill their fiduciary duty to their buyers or sellers. It’s through this lens that we make all of our decisions, including to display Realtor.com Preview Listings sourced from Zillow. … Continue reading “More Exposure, Less Fragmentation: Why Realtor.com Is Opening Preview Listings to More Buyers” Navigating the “Pre-Search” Phase with the Realtor.com App in ChatGPT by Mickey Neuberger on 30th March 2026 Today, I’m proud to share the launch of the Realtor.com app in ChatGPT. This new conversational experience helps guide consumers through the “pre-search” phase, that critical, often-overwhelming window where buyers tackle big-picture questions about affordability and lifestyle. When you’re ready to move from brainstorming to browsing, the app seamlessly transitions you to Realtor.com. There, you can immerse yourself in visuals, including videos, photos, floorplans, and our FlyAround feature, and leverage deep market insights that help you truly understand the homes you’re looking at before you connect with an agent. … Continue reading “Navigating the “Pre-Search” Phase with the Realtor.com App in ChatGPT” Sellers Deserve Clicks, Not Cliques: Why Maximum Exposure Wins by Realtor.com on 18th March 2026 Sellers want clicks , not cliques . We believe sellers are best served by maximizing exposure to their listing either as a ‘Coming Soon’ listing, or a ‘For Sale’ listing in their MLS. Sellers should be wary of advice that they should limit their advertising campaign to any one portal or brokerage, resulting in fewer buyers, when they can freely promote their property on all portals, at no cost. We understand a seller’s desire for price exploration and we believe a ‘Coming Soon’ listing is the best way to do that. Using the ‘Coming Soon’ status and advertising these properties to the full open market solves the challenge of achieving price discovery without starting the days-on-market clock and eliminates the need for private marketplaces. ‘Coming Soon’ ensures a fair marketplace where every buyer has equal access to all listings and all information about the property, and every seller has maximum exposure for their home, leading to more eyeballs, more bidders, more offers and oftentimes a higher sale price. … Continue reading “Sellers Deserve Clicks, Not Cliques: Why Maximum Exposure Wins” Realtor.com+ Expands to San Diego and San Francisco MLSs as Momentum Grows by Anna Marie Castiglioni on 9th March 2026 Just one month ago we introduced Realtor.com+ with a clear mission: to build a collaborative search platform that keeps the industry, and the agent, at the center of the experience. The response has been nothing short of incredible. I’m thrilled to share that we are already expanding Realtor.com+, signing two major California MLSs and bringing the total number of participating MLSs to 18. Building on our successful launch in January with 16 signed MLSs, the newest partners include San Diego MLS and the San Francisco Association of REALTORS ® MLS – extending our collaborative search platform into two of the nation’s most dynamic and competitive housing markets and providing 17,000 more agents with access to the Realtor.com+ tools. … Continue reading “Realtor.com+ Expands to San Diego and San Francisco MLSs as Momentum Grows” FY26 Q2 (Oct – Dec) Earnings: The Most Engaged Audience in the Industry Driving Continued Revenue Growth by Damian Eales on 5th February 2026 Strong quarterly audience and revenue In our fiscal second quarter¹, Realtor.com delivered exceptional results. According to the independent industry measure, Comscore² , we drove 3.4X the visit share of Homes.com and 2.3X Redfin, while rapidly catching Zillow by closing more than half the visit share gap over the past 18-months. We remained No. 1 in audience engagement — the measure we consider most associated with buyer intent. At 4.8 visits per unique visitor we are materially ahead of our closest competitors. Our powerful audience is increasingly a result of being part of News Corp. We expertly leverage trusted brands—including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, MarketWatch, The Sun U.S., The New York Post, and most recently, the California Post—to strategically extend our brand and content reach to generate high-intent buyers for the listings on our site. … Continue reading “FY26 Q2 (Oct – Dec) Earnings: The Most Engaged Audience in the Industry Driving Continued Revenue Growth” From Conflict to Concrete: A New Year’s Resolution by Damian Eales on 29th December 2025 Colleagues, As we approach a new year, I am asking our industry to make one resolution: let’s recommit ourselves to a shared purpose that unites us – fighting for access for the American homeowner. Ours is an industry built on problem solving. Yet, too often lately it has been beset by bickering. We have exhausted our energy debating the merits of Clear Cooperation and the demerits of private listings. These debates, while legitimate, have become distractions from larger challenges, and while we argue over how to slice a shrinking pie, millions of Americans are starving for a slice of the American Dream. It is time to trade our discord for a common chorus. We must align on the one issue that truly matters: Housing Supply. … Continue reading “From Conflict to Concrete: A New Year’s Resolution” Posts pagination Page 1 Page 2 … Page 24 Next page Search Search for: Search Welcome to Homemade, Realtor.com®’s corporate blog.
